A MESSAGE TO THE ZETA ZETA FROM
BROTHER ARCHIBALD DOUGLAS

The following is an address which was read by Colonel Harry
T. Logan, Epsilon Phi '07, prior to the closing of the Installa
tion ceremonies of the Zeta Zeta Chapter at the University,
British Columbia, which had been sent on by President Archi
bald Douglas who unfortunately, at the last moment, found it
impossible to leave New York City owing to pressing business.

WISH that I had been with you, today, to have taken part in the

I impressive ceremonies of your installation. To my intense regret,
I could not be. We have delegated Brothers Charles A. Spooner
and Bourke Corcoran, devoted members of our Executive Council for
many years and whose services to Psi Upsilon are almost numberless,
to represent us at your installation. They are worthy of this great
honor. They will, on our behalf, welcome you ardently into our Fra
ternity, to our brotherhood of University and College men that had its
beginnings over a century ago at Union College on the banks of the
Mohawk in the State of New York. They will carry a greeting and
welcome that comes to you all from your twenty-seven sister chapters
and from the many thousands of your Brothers scattered over the
United States and Canada and throughout the World. They reach out
to you the right hand of brotherhood and their hearts throb in tune
with yours and ours on this notable occasion.

History of Expansion
At old Union College, seven men 

undergraduates 

founded this
Fraternity and the Theta Chapter in 1833. Their work was good but
they builded far better than they knew. Since those early days, one by
one, chapters have been added whose members clasped hands, sang our
songs and wore our symbols. Each succeeding chapter strengthened and
cemented us in the spirit of fraternal loyalty and friendship as you do
now. Following the Theta, the Delta was installed at New York Uni

versity on this far Atlantic and through the New England and Eastern
States, other chapters followed. At Yale, Brown, Dartmouth and Co
lumbia, and our far eastern chapter at Bowdoin, Maine, in 1843. Then,
in order, at Hamilton, Wesleyan, Harvard and Rochester, until in
1860, we ventured as far west as Ohio when the Iota of Kenyon signed

4 THE DIAMOND OF PSI UPSILON

our rolls, afterwards, with the Phi of Michigan and the Omega of Chi
cago, we were fast becoming nationalized; so, in succession, charters
were granted to chapters at
Cornell, Trinity, Lehigh, the University of
Pennsylvania, Minnesota and Wisconsin until in 1902, with the Epsilon
of the University of California, we first "looked upon the Pacific";
then came the Omicron at Illinois, the Delta Delta at Williams and your
neighbor and intimate friend on the South, the Theta Theta of Wash
ington until when the University of Toronto covenanted with us, we
happily became international. The result proved so highly satisfactory^
to us all that the Epsilon Phi followed at McGill and now with the
Zeta Zeta at Vancouver, our Canadian chapters hold our fraternal out
posts on the north and northwest. So you are the last of a long and
illustrious line of chapters reaching from the Atlantic to the Pacific
and from Maine to Vancouver. "Last but not least," the Zeta Zeta
makes our Psi U world complete and it is doubtful if another
chapter
will be added for many years.
Thus, you have become joint heritors with us of the stimulating
traditions, aspirations and ideals that built up over a century of in
numerable and immemorial Psi U friendships which have come down to
us from an ever
increasing past to carry them on into an auspicious fu
ture.
The torch lit at the altar of the Theta on Founders
Day 1833 has
just lit the torch of this far chapter of the Zeta Zeta in our sister nation
in 1935. On you and on all of
us, your Brothers, now and always rests
the joint and happy obligation
through all the coming years to keep
the light of Psi Upsilon burning bright.

Purposes Have Not Changed
The essential purposes of our
Fraternity have not changed in over
a century. Its basis is the bringing together of companionable minds;
the friendship of men drawn together by mutual ties and interests.
In all the theory of selection
applies. Comradeship first brought the old
Theta group together. As youthful
comrades, they entered into pledges
that young men selected by them or their
successors with the same
ideals of fraternal
friendship in turn entered into. The "thoughts of
youth" in 1833 were "long, long thoughts."
There is nothing in the wide world that more
_
entrances the imagina
tion than to look back and to
try to picture those young men our
pioneers of early days, now gone, who year by
year, decade on decade,

THE DIAMOND OF PSI UPSILON 5

went out from our Universities and Colleges invigorated by and finer
for ourbrotherhood. Would that we had a composite photograph of
them all! The rare face so pictured would show culture and purpose,
honor, character and resolution; humor and discernment; and frank
eyes for fine friendships. Among those making up that composite
would be statesmen and jurists; men of peace and men of war; men of
letters and of law; leaders in medicine and in reUgious and educational
thought; scientists and inventors; poets and practitioners; doers and
dreamers sage in many things and true in all. Men of credit to their

nations, their times, to their Colleges and to themselves. All knowing
the finer amenities of life through the grip of Psi U hands.
Nor has our past a monopoly on all this for I venture to say apart
from the more formal dress of years ago, the composite of today would
pass for that of yesterday.
Another hundred years awaits us. With the assured devotion of
"brothers old and young," we go forward into our future. For the Psi U
tie is not brief nor passing with the closing of our College doors ^it

should be and is lifelong.
Take the fine tradition of Psi Upsilon with you as a proud heritage
and inspiration and carry on!
And now, for our Psi U Brothers, everywhere, we give you, under
graduate and graduate Brothers of the Zeta Zeta:
Hail and Welcome 

Let Us Go Onward Together!
ARCHIBALD DOUGLAS
President of the Executive Council
of the Psi Upsilon Fraternity

ZETA ZETA CHAPTER INSTALLED AT THE
UNIVERSITY OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

MANY BROTHERS PRESENT AS ALPHA KAPPA
ALPHA FORMALLY BECOMES A
CHAPTER OF PSI UPSILON

chapter of Psi Upsilon, known as the Zeta Zeta Chapter,
ANEW was installed at the

October 19, 1935.
University of British Columbia on Saturday,

After eight years of petitioning, the local society of Alpha Kappa
Alpha secured the unanimous ratification vote of all chapters to their
petition as a result of the action taken at the 1935 convention held with
the Beta Beta Chapter late in April.
With a total attendance of nearly 200 including the 62 initiates, a
gala week end of festivities marked the inauguration of this, our third
chapter in Canada and, likewise, our third chapter on the Pacific Coast.
Practically the entire membership of the active chapter at the Uni
versity of Washington together with a great number of their Alumni and
Alumni of other chapters resident in Seattle, journeyed to Vancouver
for these exercises.
The delegates from the Executive Council were : Charles P. Spooner,
Rho '94, and R. Bourke Corcoran, Omega '15. Also present from the
East: Edward L. Stevens, Chi '99 (for 22 years a member of the Execu
tive Council and the last five years of which he was its President), and
Clarence L. Von Egloff stein, Delta '12.

The program of the week-end was as follows :

Friday afternoon October 18, 1935:

Registration at the Vancouver Hotel, Vancouver, British Colum
bia.
8:00 P.M.Smoker, Psi Upsilon fraternity sing, and entertainment.

Saturday October 19, 1935:
11:00 A.M. Formal installation ceremonies, Vancouver Hotel.

1:30 P.M. ^Luncheon given by the Psi Upsilon Alumni Associa

tion of Vancouver.
4 to 6:00 P.M. 

Tea and Reception given by the Zeta Zeta Chap
ter in the Oval Room of the Vancouver Hotel.
7 :30 P.M. 

Installation Banquet.

THE DIAMOND OF PSI UPSILON 7

The Installation

The formal ritual for the installation of a new chapter of Psi Upsilon
was conducted by Brother Corcoran, assisted by Brothers Stevens, Gor
don McLaren, Nu '13, Colonel Harry T. Logan, Epsilon Phi '07, and the
senior delegates from the chapters at the University of California and
the University of Washington.
Also present on the platform were the following: Charles P. Spooner,
Rho '94; Lewis Schwager, Mu '95; David Whitcomb, Gamma '00;
Judge Alexander I. Fisher, Nu '01; Dr. George T. Wilson, Epsilon Phi
'10; Clarence L. Von Egloffstein, Delta '12; Wallace Collins, Beta '26;
Oliver H. Haskell, Theta Theta '26; Harry M. Boyce, Epsilon Phi '30.
Following the formal ceremonies. Brother Corcoran presented a
number of gifts to the new chapter on behalf of the Executive Council
and of the individual donors. These included:
A silk Psi U flag, flag pole and standard from Brother Eugene S.
Wilson, Gamma '02.
Antique Bronze Owl from Brother Walter T. Collins, Iota '02.
Large oil painting from the Zeta Chapter and its Alumni depicting
the coat-of-arms of the Fraternity in the middle panel, coat-of-arms of
the Zeta Chapter in one side panel and the coat-of-arms of the Zeta Zeta
Chapter in the other side panel.
An outdoor wool bunting Psi Upsilon flag and ballot box from the
Theta Theta Chapter.
A handsome morocco bound minute book from the Epsilon Chapter.
A beautiful morocco bound guest autograph album and register from
the Psi U Alumni of Vancouver.
A hand illuminated Charter signed by the members of the Executive
Council and presented by Brother Archibald Douglas, Lambda '94.
Anebony and silver gavel and stand presented by Brother R. Bourke
Corcoran, Omega 'IS.
A pair of silver candlesticks from the Epsilon Phi Chapter.
History of the Xi Chapter from the Xi autographed by the author,
Karl P. Harrington, Xi '82.
A book entitled "Occasions in Psi Upsilon" autographed by the
author, Earl D. Babst, Iota-Phi '93.
In addition to these gifts there were the Bronze Founders' Tablet
presented by the Executive Council and the usual song books, song
rec

ords, bound copies of The Diamond, two magnificently bound copies of

8 THE DIAMOND OF PSI UPSILON

the Constitution and a number of other items normally presented by the
Fraternity to a new chapter.
Quoting from a letter received since the installation, written by
Colonel Harry T. Logan, Professor of Classics at the University of
British Columbia, Nu '01, he says:

"It is all a very grand show to look back upon. Nothing could
have been finer than the friendly spirit of all the delegates and the
magnificent attendance from the Theta Theta Chapter. It is a good
omen for the future association of these two chapters. Today's

mail brought a fine letter from the chapter at Washington to our
new chapter, the Zeta Zeta. The general spirit of welcome and the

atmosphere of the installation created by the wealth of gifts and
the sentiments of the ceremony, especially the address of our Pres
ident, Archibald Douglas, was a very splendid introduction for the
new chapter. I shall not soon forget the shrine song at the con

clusion of the ceremony, it was most moving."

Full recital of the informal talks given at the delightfully intimate
and informal luncheon are printed elsewhere in this issue as are the
addresses made at the formal installation banquet. The settings for these
two affairs were indeed ideal and
gave every evidence of the careful
planning of the Brothers, old and young, of Vancouver. Psi Upsilon
colors predominated.
The Tea and Reception held in the Oval Room of the Vancouver
Hotel from four to six o'clock was an unusually delightful affair. Invi
tations had been extended to members of the University
Senate, the
faculty, mothers, wives and sweethearts of the members, old and new,
and to representatives of the other organizations at the
University of
British Columbia. Approximately 300 people were present at this
gather
ing where, in addition to the music of a stringed orchestra, the Brothers
sang a number of Psi Upsilon songs in toast to the ladies and other
guests present.
Thus, with the installation completed, and all the ceremonies, lunch
eons and banquets over, the Zeta Zeta Chapter takes its place on the
honored chapter roll of Psi Upsilon.
Our Fraternity has great cause to be very proud of its newest
chap
ter. Psi Upsilon expects and knows she will receive from our Zeta Zeta

Chapter many real achievements.

PROCEEDINGS AT LUNCHEON
HOTEL VANCOUVER, OCTOBER 19, 1935

luncheon was served in the Oak Room of the Hotel Van

BUFFET couver after the installation ceremony which was finished about
1:00 P.M. At the luncheon the initiates, the visiting delegates,
and representatives of the University of British Columbia were guests
of the Psi Upsilon Alumni of Vancouver.
After the luncheon a few brief speeches were made.
Lt.-Col. Harry T. Logan {Chairman) :
We are going to have one or two welcoming speeches from visiting
delegates, and from members of the University of British Columbia.
The first will be a message of welcome by Dr. Sage, Professor of History,
who has been delegated by the President of the University, who is not
able to be here this afternoon, and who has asked Dr. Sage to say a
few words of welcome to Psi Upsilon Fraternity.
Dr. Sage:
Brothers: President Klinck regrets exceedingly that he is unable
to be present with us on this glad occasion; and he has deputed me to

give a word of welcome from the youngest University in Canada to one
of the oldest International fraternities.
The University of British Columbia opened its doors for the first
time in 1915. When you saw our boys going through the ceremony this
morning you must have noticed that on the gowns they wore there was
a khaki cord. That khaki cord is on the gown of the undergraduate of

the University of B.C. Why is it there? It is a reminder for all time
that, in the history of the University, we started during the period of the
Great War. Our University's infancy was therefore in troublous times.
When the Richmond herald-at-arms made up the coat of arms of
the University of British Columbia he gave us a motto which is a chal
lenge to every member of the University. "Tuum est" (It is thine), but
more hterally translated, "It is up to you," and during our twenty years
existence we have had great co-operation between the faculty and the
student body. That is why you who visited the University, or who will
visit it this afternoon, wiU see there the cairn. Our university life is
centered around that cairn in front of the Science Building, and not far
from the bus terminus. And why? Because lying at the base of that cairn
is the petition of sixty thousand people of British Columbia to the Gov-

10 the diamond of psi upsilon

ernment of British Columbia to build the University, and securing
that petition was the work of the undergraduates and graduates.
On the occasion of the march of the students to the site at Point
Grey, where the skeleton of the Science Building had already whitened
for eight years in the winter rains and had been blown upon by the
March winds, I was privileged to stand beside the Chancellor, Dr.
McKechnie. He told me that when he was at old McGill he had dreamed
of becoming a professor, but now he was the Chancellor of the Univer
sity. The University of British Columbia is in a real sense the child of
old McGill and as a Toronto man I wish to say that we owe a deep
debt of gratitude to McGill for establishing her university college in
British Columbia and to the devoted group which founded and taught
in the college.
My Brothers, the University of British Columbia welcomes Psi
Upsilon. It is a great day. We of the university realize that the coming
of Psi Upsilon to our campus is one of the good things that has happened
in the history of the university. We trust that Zeta Zeta will be a worthy
link in the chain of Psi Upsilon.

Chairman :
Brother Charlie Spooner will say a word on behalf of Psi U.

Brother Spooner:

I hardly know what to say on the very gracious and delightful wel
come that has been given the Fraternity. The Fraternity is delighted to
be here, but do not think for a moment that because you are
glad and
proud to have it here, that the Fraternity is not quite humble in many
ways in coming in here. The reason is this: That while we are proud of
our Fraternity and its
age, and what it has accomplished, our experi
ence with McGill and with Toronto, and we expect with this Chapter

here, will show us certain things that we otherwise would not have found
out, and so far as I am concerned, and speaking for Psi Upsilon, we are
very glad to be here.
The underlying reason is this: We have too many college
students, a
lot of us think, in the United States; too many people
trying to get an
education which a great many people in the United States think
they.
would be better without, and the net result is, sadly
enough, that edu
cation is more and more not being taken seriously enough by the
average
of our academic students. We found at McGill a different situation

THE DIAMOND OF PSI UPSILON 11

altogether. I remember distinctly at our last Convention with our Hamil
ton Chapter, Charlie Davis (I suppose most of
you people have never
met him) ; he came before the convention at Hamilton in that delightful

way of his and spoke a few words and asked if anyone wanted to ask a
few questions.
I asked him what the rate of mortality had been in the petitioning
society. He stroked his chin and said, "I don't believe I know just what
you mean." I said, "what percentage of those who join the Epsilon Phi
as Freshmen fail to graduate?" "Why," he said, "I don't seem to re

member anybody that has ever joined who did not finally graduate." He
said, "There may have been one, but I am not sure about that." It cer
tainly was a joke to him to have an inquiry made about the rate of
mortality. On the other hand it is a regrettable fact that in some of
the chapters they initiate ten or fifteen freshmen and from one cause or
another they leak out until there seem to be only four or five in the
graduating class. This is gradually being stopped. We have made strenu
ous efforts not to have that happen.

We have found in our contact with Psi Upsilon Brothers since the
first chapters were taken in in Canada that you fellows above the line up
here seem to take the business of being educated a lot more seriously
than most of our fellows. Unfortunately a great many of the young
people over in our country go to colleges for reasons that I doubt if any
of your boys and girls go to college ^viz. for social reasons. Their

parents are not educated themselves but they want their sons and
daughters to be educated, not so much for what education really means,
but for the social position and prestige they think goes with education. I
may be wrong about it, but I just cannot conceive of your students up
here north of the line going for any such purposes. The English are
less superficial than we are in the United States. Of course they are a
great deal older. I have always thought that the English and Canadian
were about as fine a type as there was in the world, and I still think so.

I have played with them and have always found they are good sports.
I shall never forget what the fellows told me about the men who were
called remittance men over in Victoria and Vancouver; that the minute
the war came they could not get in fast enough. Some have come back
minus a leg or an arm, and some have never come back.
The Fraternity has a lot to get from you, and I hope that no faults
of ours or our Universities on the other side of the line will have an
insidious effect in dropping your standard, because personally I look

12 THE DIAMOND OF PSI UPSILON

upon McGill, Toronto

and I am sure it will hold with the University
of B. C. and our Chapter here as influences that will assist the Execu

tive Council in raising the standard of the undergraduates in our Fra
ternity. The records of your Chapter here which your local society has
given to us from time to time, give evidence that your members conform
to a similar type of undergraduate as is found at the Eastern Canadian
Universities. So, while I am delighted on behalf of the Fraternity to
receive the delightful welcome that has just been tendered us, I want
to express as far as I am personally concerned that we should be grateful
that we are coming in here, because our experience in the Canadian
Universities that we have chapters in has shown us that our general
standard is raised by the admission of the Canadian chapters.
Another thing that I am glad we are in for is the inculcation of the
British sense of humour. I have mixed an awful lot with the English
and I love their sense of humour. I heard a story a short time ago which
illustrates this characteristic in a striking way. An American in London
was riding along Oxford Street on the top of an old-fashioned horse-bus

about eight o'clock in the morning, and there was no one else on the bus.
As they approached another bus coming from the opposite direction the
driver shouted at the driver of the other bus and took out a string with a
noose on it, a few inches long. He dangled it in front of the other driver

until he passed out of sight. The other driver called him everything he
could think of until he passed on. "Why did you dangle that in front
of him, and why did he get so angry?" the American asked. "Well," he
said, "his governor was hung this morning, and I wanted to see if the
blighter had a sense of humour."
Now we have both kinds of humour in our Fraternity.

Chairman :
Thank you. Brother Spooner. I am going to ask Professor Barss to
say a few welcoming words to the new Chapter. Professor Barss is

the faculty representative on the Interfraternity Council and as such he
represents the fraternities on the campus. He himself is a member of
one of the oldest fraternities 

I think a year older than ours Alpha

Delta Phi.

Professor Barss:
Mr. Chairman and Gentlemen: It would be a very natural
thing
to say "Brothers," as your Chairman does. I have
already had several
attempts to hand me the grip 

this is an innocent evidence of a f riendli-

THE DIAMOND OF PSI UPSILON 13

ness which I appreciate. You need not worry, as I will
give no secrets
away.
I would like first to congratulate
you on my own behalf, on this step
which has been taken today in the initiation of the local
group of Alpha
Kappa Alpha into Psi Upsilon. I also feel that as Professor of Horticul
ture I should compliment you on the circumstances which occasion such
an attractive horticultural
display as I see in the lapels of your coats.
I would like, too, just as an Alpha
Delt, to say how pleased I am to have
this particular body come to this campus. While Alpha Delta Phi seems
to have shown the way in point of years since its establishment and has
set the example in coming to this campus, if my 29 years of
fraternity
life and associations with other chapters of Psi Upsilon may be used as
a gauge, I feel confident that the two
groups are going to work together
very, very happily at this University.
You may be interested to learn that it so happens that I was a Chair
man of the committee on the University Senate that dealt with this

problem of whether or not fraternities should be allowed on this campus.
The committee went into the question thoroughly and seriously, and
eventually hopefully arranged that fraternities should be given official
recognition, feeling that in the fraternities there was the possibility of a
source of great strength to the University.

Your Chairman has asked me particularly to speak on behalf of
the fraternities on the campus. I do, therefore, here and now, most
heartily congratulate you, and welcome this new Chapter of Psi Upsilon
as the youngest International on the campus. At the same time, it

scarcely seems to be a new group, because these men have for years
as a local fraternity been taking an active part in University life.

For those who may not know, I might explain that we have on the
campus ten fraternities besides the Jewish fraternities, and an Inter
fraternity Council on which I happen to be the present Faculty Repre
sentative. Incidentally, it had to be Psi U to show the way, for Col.
Logan was the faculty member who preceded me on that Council. One
thing I like to think, after having served for some four years as repre
sentative of the faculty on that Council, is that the fraternities more
and more realize that they have a function to perform in the University.
All fraternities, whether they realize it or not, as they come into
being and exist in a University, exist only by virtue of the continued
existence of that University. In actual fact, a Fraternity could be char
acterized by the rather unattractive word "Parasite," inasmuch as its

14 THE DIAMOND OF PSI UPSILON

own life depends solely on the existence of its host, the University. But
fortunately there are two types of parasites one being that which gains

its strength at the expense of its host (a type which I confidentially
trust does not describe our own groups). The other type is that which,
while a true parasite in that it lives by virtue of the host to which it is
attached, does actually in turn contribute toward the well-being of its
host in other words, they live together to their mutual benefit.

I feel sure, friends, that this latter describes the relationship which
exists and will continue to exist between the University of British
Columbia and the fraternities on the campus; the fraternities definitely
striving to aid the University to attain its objective in the realm of
higher education.
Now just a word in closing. Fraternities as they first came to this
campus had the feeling, I am sure, that the chief aim and object of the
fraternity must necessarily be largely competitive self -maintenance.
I am happy today in believing that the fraternities on our campus have
quite outgrown this idea, but instead are enjoying harmonious associa
tion together, each honestly striving to get down to the normal life and
function of the fraternity in the University.
As was true of this group in its former life as Alpha Kappa Alpha,
so may it continue to be true of the new group, Psi Upsilon, that the

members may live together happily, healthily, helpfully, working for
the betterment, not just of themselves, but of the University in which
they are to exist.
And so on behalf of your fellow fraternities on the campus, I again
congratuate you, wish you success, and welcome you back into the fold
in your new-found relationship in Psi Upsilon.

Chairman :

When Professor Barss almost used the word "brother," I thought
that we were going to be let in to some of the Alpha Delta Phi secrets,
but he went on to assure us that this was not the case : there would be
nobetrayal of secrets on either side. This is as it should be. I am going
to ask Dr. Douglas Telford, one of the oldest charter members of
Alpha
Kappa Alpha, to speak on behalf of the new chapter, Zeta Zeta.
Dr. Telford:

Brothers of Psi Upsilon: I cannot rival Dr. Sage in years of experi
ence, nor in years of maturity, but I do say that we appreciate what

the diamond of PSI UPSILON 15

Dr. Barss has said. He speaks to us as member of the faculty, and what
he says, I know, is sincere. He is also an Alpha Delta Phi, and we very
graciouly rank Alpha Delta Phi on a par with Psi Upsilon. Dr. Barss
is the type of man to whom we would like to give the hand-shake of Psi
Upsilon had he not been an Alpha Delta Phi. I wish to say that we as a
fraternity on the campus will try with all our powers to be a real working
unit within the University, and we realize that we depend upon the
University for our existence. We will strive at it too because we love our
University, and because it has given birth to us. I do want to say too
that we appreciate the welcome you have given us, Dr. Barss, and that
we will do everything in our power to show that we appreciate this wel

come.

This afternoon there is a tea reception, to which the Senate, the
Faculty, and others are invited, and we extend an invitation to you and
to other associations in Vancouver to be present. I do repeat then that
we appreciate this message of welcome from you. Dr. Barss.
Chairman :

Before asking Brother Pollock to say a few words, may I say, speak
ing on behalf of the Vancouver Alumni of Psi Upsilon, how very much
we have appreciated this ceremony today, and also, although or rather

because we are very small in numbers, how very much we appreciate

Greeks and Romans Had Emblems
In the early agesindividuals, families and tribes adopted various
emblems and symbols to serve as their- particular marks of distinction.
That they might be easily identified in battle, these marks were placed
on ensigns and shields. The Greeks and Romans, and other early na

tions assigned various emblems to individuals and to their deities.
When heraldic emblems were first used, there was little or no defi
nite scheme for the adaption or arrangement of the symbols. Later, there
were certain legislative enactments in various countries which brought

Heraldry to a systematic and scientific basis. The color schemes, de
signs, symbols, metals and furs used on the shields were originally pur
ported to be suggestive of deeds of valor, ideals or aims. Individuals
and families who gave allegiance to another, sometimes adopted the
Coat-of-Arms of the latter with some alterations to show respect and
possibly class distinction.
In addition to being used by families and individuals, armorial bear
ings came to be used by towns and cities, corporations, hotels and other
institutions such as Colleges, Universities and Societies. Today, the use
of armorial bearings which most nearly conforms to the historic and

Dr. Frank Swift Bourns, Phi '90
Dr. Bourns, one of the most beloved Alumni of the
Fraternity resi
dent in Seattle, Washington, died on March 17 last. He had lived in
Seattle for the past thirty years where he was
widely known as x-ray
and radium specialist.

trip to the Philippines as a member of a scientific
expedition interested in ornithology.

the islands in 1893, and through his work there became a close friend of

there on the Philippine Commission after the Spanish American War.

for he had been a staunch backer of the local society during its years of
petitioning for a charter. After the chapter was established in 1916, he
was one of its devoted and loyal "older Brothers."

of Psi Us in the Northwest."
